2027-05-11.title: Tuesday of the Seventh Week of Easter
readings: I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus
Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth (or: Alleluia)
Father, glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you
2027-05-11.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. From today until Thursday the Gospels are taken from the prayer of Jesus at the Last Supper (John 17), the “priestly prayer.” The novena to the Holy Spirit continues.
2027-05-11.verse: And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
theo: Paul is on his way to Jerusalem, hurrying to arrive before Pentecost (Acts 20:16). His ship stops at Miletus, a port about fifty kilometres south of Ephesus, and he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church. When they arrive he speaks to them as a father who knows he will not see his children again. This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christian leaders, and it is his farewell. He looks back first: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the entire time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears.” He reminds them of the trials he endured, including plots by those who opposed him, and of how he held nothing back: “I did not shrink from doing anything helpful, proclaiming the message to you and teaching you publicly and from house to house.” His message was simple and complete: “repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus,” to Jews and Greeks alike.

Then he looks ahead: “as a captive to the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and persecutions are waiting for me.” Paul does not know the details, only the direction. And he is at peace: “I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of God's grace.” The word “course” is the runner's track; Paul sees his life as a race to be run to the end. He can say, with a clear conscience, “I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.” Not a selection of pleasant truths, but the whole of it. The Psalm gives thanks to the God “who daily bears us up,” and to whom “belongs escape from death”: that is the confidence with which Paul walks towards chains.

In the Gospel we hear the beginning of the great prayer of Jesus. “He looked up to heaven and said, ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you.’” The hour is the cross, and Jesus calls it glory: the moment when the love of the Father and the Son is most fully shown. Then he defines eternal life, not as endless time but as a relationship: “this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” To know, in the Bible, is to love and be united. Jesus can say what Paul will echo at Miletus: “I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.” And he prays for his disciples: “I am asking on their behalf … because they are yours … And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you.” These are words of the Ascension. Jesus goes to the Father, and he leaves his friends in the world, held in his prayer. Paul at Miletus, handing his flock to God, is praying the same prayer in his own way.
conn: An ancient Ionian port at the mouth of the river Maeander, south of Ephesus. Paul chose not to go into Ephesus itself, perhaps to save time or to avoid trouble (Acts 20:16).
In Greek presbyteroi; in verse 28 Paul also calls them episkopoi, overseers, and tells them to shepherd the church of God. From these words come our words priest and bishop.
Paul speaks of his tears twice in this speech (Acts 20:19, 31) and also in his letters (2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18). His ministry was not cold administration but love that wept.
The first Christians met in homes (Acts 2:46; Romans 16:5). Paul taught both in public places and in family gatherings.
Literally “bound in the Spirit.” Before he is bound with chains in Jerusalem, Paul is already bound by obedience to the Spirit.
An image from the athletic games. Near the end of his life Paul will write: “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

The name given to John 17 since the sixteenth-century Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus, but its content was recognized by the Fathers: Jesus, as High Priest, consecrates himself and prays for his disciples and for all who will believe.
In John, glory (doxa) is the visible radiance of God's love. The cross is the hour of glory because there love is shown without limit (John 12:23–24; 13:31–32).
In biblical language knowledge is personal communion, as in Jeremiah 9:24 and Hosea 6:6. Eternal life begins now, in knowing and loving God.
altar: In the priestly prayer Jesus offers himself to the Father for his disciples. At every Mass that same offering is made present: the Son glorifies the Father by giving himself, and we, joined to him, are offered with him.

Paul said he did not shrink from declaring the whole purpose of God. The Mass, too, holds nothing back: the Lord gives us his whole self, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, so that we may know him, and in knowing him have eternal life.
outline: Ask: if you knew you were seeing your family or parish for the last time, what would you say to them?

live: Think of one truth or kindness you have kept from someone because it was uncomfortable. Offer it today, gently.
Look at one duty you are tempted to leave unfinished. Finish it today, as an offering to the Lord.
Spend ten minutes today with John 17:1–11, not to study it but to listen to Jesus praying for you.
fathers: This is eternal life: to know God. The knowledge that saves is not the knowledge of many things, but the knowledge of God that is joined to love. We shall be fully happy when we see him as he is; even now we begin to live by knowing him.
See how Paul, about to depart, does not boast of miracles but of tears and labours. He shows the elders a shepherd who wept for his flock day and night; this is the model he leaves them.
St Gregory the Great (Pastoral Rule, in substance)
The shepherd must not keep silent out of fear or flattery. He must not hide the truth from those entrusted to him, but declare the whole counsel of God, with discretion and love.
magis: When his hour came, Jesus prayed to the Father; his prayer at the Last Supper, the priestly prayer, embraces the whole economy of creation and salvation, his death and Resurrection.

The priestly prayer of Jesus fulfils, from within, the great petitions of the Lord's Prayer: concern for the Father's name, zeal for his kingdom, the accomplishment of his will, and deliverance from evil.
The ministerial priesthood is a service. It is entirely related to Christ and to the faithful; it depends on Christ and his unique priesthood.
God is truthful when he reveals himself; his teaching is true instruction, and the Son came into the world “to testify to the truth.”
Whoever does not know God, even though he may entertain all kinds of hopes, is ultimately without hope; true life is relationship with him who is the source of life.
saints: A Capuchin lay brother of Sardinia (1701–1781) who for some forty years went begging alms for his friary through the streets of Cagliari. Known for his gentleness and his care for the poor and sick, he was canonized in 1951. The Capuchins keep his memory on 11 May.
From 1956 to 1969 the feast of Sts Philip and James was kept on 11 May; since the calendar reform of 1969 it has been celebrated on 3 May.
2027-05-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, when your hour came, you lifted up your eyes to heaven and prayed for your friends. Pray for us now, as you go to the Father. Teach us that eternal life is to know the only true God and you whom he has sent; let us know you, love you and be one with you. Give us the heart of Paul, who served you with humility and tears, held nothing back from your people, and ran his course to the end. Bless all pastors of your Church, that they may shepherd your flock faithfully and declare the whole purpose of God. Keep us in your name while we remain in the world, and send us your Holy Spirit, for whom we wait with Mary. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: At Miletus Paul said farewell to the elders of Ephesus: he had served with humility and tears and held nothing back.
He was going to Jerusalem, bound by the Spirit, willing to lose his life if only he could finish his course.
Jesus prayed: Father, the hour has come; this is eternal life, to know you and the one you have sent.
2027-05-11.action: Finish today one task or duty you have been tempted to leave half done, and offer it to the Lord.
2027-05-11.question: Do I see eternal life as something far away, or as knowing and loving God now?
kidsaint: Ignatius was a Capuchin brother on the island of Sardinia in Italy. Every day for forty years he walked the streets with a bag, asking for food for the friars and for the poor. He was always gentle and smiling, and he helped sick people and children he met on the way. Lesson: even a simple job, done with love every day, can make you a saint.
2027-05-11.special: Easter weekday; the Gospels from today until Thursday come from the priestly prayer of Jesus (John 17). Novena to the Holy Spirit. Regina Caeli at noon.
term: From the Greek presbyteros, “elder”: in the New Testament a leader of a local church (Acts 20:17). Our word “priest” comes from it. Priests share in the ministry of the bishop as his co-workers.

family.explain: Before he died, Jesus looked up to heaven and prayed to his Father for his friends. He said that eternal life means knowing God, not just knowing about him, but loving him and being his friend. Jesus prays for us too, every day, from heaven.
family.intention: We pray for our parish priest and for all priests, and for missionaries who have left their homes for Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we get to know Jesus better as a family?” Choose one way, such as reading a short Gospel passage after dinner, and try it this week.

illus: When an old priest in a hill parish in Idukki was transferred after eighteen years, the church was full for his farewell Mass. He did not speak about the buildings he had put up. He said: I tried to tell you the whole truth, even when you did not like it, and I tried to visit every house. If I failed anyone, forgive me. Then he asked the people to pray for the new priest. Afterwards an old woman who had often argued with him said: he scolded us, but he wept for us too. We always knew he loved us.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you pray for us to the Father. Let us know you and the Father, and so have eternal life. Come, Holy Spirit. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Serving the Lord with all humility and with tears (Acts 20:19). Whom do I serve with real love, even when it costs me?
If only I may finish my course (Acts 20:24). What is the course the Lord has given me, and am I running it?
This is eternal life, that they may know you (John 17:3). How well do I know God, not only about him?
pm.resp: Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth.
interc: For bishops and priests, that they may shepherd the Church with humility, courage and love, holding nothing back.
For missionaries who have left home for the Gospel, and for those who suffer imprisonment for their faith.
For those facing the last part of their life's course, that they may finish it with faith and peace.
For all who seek God, that they may come to know him and Jesus Christ whom he has sent.
For our group, that we may be kept in the name of the Father and receive the Holy Spirit.
pm.close: Father, your Son prayed that we may know you and be kept in your name. Grant that we may finish our course with joy and come to eternal life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today we stand on the beach at Miletus and listen to a farewell. Paul has called the elders of Ephesus, and he speaks to them for the last time. What does he remember? Not his success, not his miracles, but this: I served the Lord with all humility and with tears (Acts 20:19).

He tells them: I did not shrink from doing anything helpful; I taught you publicly and from house to house. I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole purpose of God (Acts 20:20, 27). Paul did not give his people only the easy parts of the Gospel. He gave them all of it, because he loved them.

Then he looks ahead. He is going to Jerusalem, and he does not know exactly what will happen, only that chains are waiting. Yet he says: I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course (Acts 20:24). Paul sees his life as a race. What matters is not how long it is, but that it is finished well.

Each of us has a course to run. A mother, a farmer, a student, a priest, a sick person in bed: each has a ministry received from the Lord Jesus. The question is not whether it is easy, but whether we will finish it with faith.

In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays: Father, the hour has come. And he tells us what eternal life is: this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). Eternal life is not only after death. It begins now, when we know God, not just about him, but as a friend knows a friend.

Jesus says: I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. These are Ascension words. He has gone to the Father, but he has not stopped praying for us. In these days before Pentecost, let us let him pray for us, and let us run our course to the end, with the Holy Spirit as our strength. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, St Paul had to say goodbye to his friends in Ephesus. He told them: I loved you, I taught you everything about Jesus, and I even cried for you. Now I must go where God sends me.
Jesus prayed to his Father for his friends, and he prays for you too. He wants you to know God as your best friend. Say: Jesus, I want to know you more!

intro: Theme: “This is eternal life, that they may know you.”
Paul's farewell at Miletus, a life run to the finish, and the prayer of Jesus for his own as he goes to the Father.

sub: Publicly and from house to house.
q: He has told you, O mortal, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
I did not shrink from doing anything helpful, proclaiming the message to you and teaching you publicly and from house to house,
points.apply: Visit or call one family of your parish or neighbourhood this week, simply to share faith and friendship.

points.h: If only I may finish my course
sub: A race run to the end.
q: So teach us to count our days that we may gain a wise heart.
But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of God’s grace.
points.apply: Name the ministry the Lord has given you in your present state of life, and finish one neglected part of it this week.

q: but let those who boast boast in this, that they understand and know me, that I am the Lord; I act with steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth, for in these things I delight, says the Lord.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
points.apply: Read John 17 slowly once this week, and let Jesus pray for you.

concl: Paul, leaving Ephesus, gave his people all of the Gospel with humility and tears, and walked towards chains wanting only to finish his course.
Jesus, going to the Father, prays for us who remain in the world; eternal life begins now, in knowing and loving the Father and the Son through the Holy Spirit.
2027-05-11.resolve: Finish one neglected duty this week as an offering to the Lord, and pray John 17 slowly before Pentecost.
